newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission formally warns VW over Italian market.
newsitem.headline: Commission formally warns VW over Italian market.

text.p: The European Commission said on Thursday it had sent Volkswagen AG and its subsidiary Audi a statement of objections over distribution restrictions in the Italian market.
The statement follows inspections carried out a year ago at the companies' premises in Germany and at their common Italian distributor called Autogerma.
Volkswagen, which is already embroiled in another EU dispute over subsidies promised by the German state of Saxony, has until mid-January to reply.
At stake in the current dispute is the alledged refusal by the distributors of Volkswagen and Audi cars in Italy to sell to Austrian, German and French buyers.

The Commission has received "many complaints from consumers alleging that Volkswagen and Audi have developed a strategy, with the complicity of their Italian partners, to prevent consumers...from buying cheaper cars in Italy," the Commission said in a statement.

Commission surveys on car prices in the European Union have shown that Italy is one of the cheapest places to buy a car due to a large extent to the depreciation of the lira after its ejection from the EU's monetary grid in 1992.
Austria, Germany and France, on the other hand, are among the most expensive markets.

Under a block exemption regulation, 1475/95/EEC, which exempts cars distribution from competition rules, carmakers are allowed to conclude exclusive dealership agreements, but consumers must be able to buy the car they want wherever it is the cheapest.

The Commission warned Volkswagen it may loose the benefit of the block exemption for the whole European Union if it persists with its restrictive practices in Italy. It could also ultimately be fined.
The Commission had already made it known, first in October 1995 and this summer, that it would not tolerate VW's selling restrictions in Italy.
Italy's price advantage, however, is slowly shrinking due to the recent appreciation of the lira, now likely to be accentuated by its return to the EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism.
